chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: First pianists to impress him: Earl Hines and Fats Waller's pipe organ
summary: He first heard Earl Hines with Louis Dippo's Pittsburgh orchestra, and had Fats Waller's 1926 Victor pipe organ record.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Now we can go on to get to some piano players that you've known.
You just go ahead and mention some piano players, Butter. You talk for a while.

Well, one of the first pianists -- this will surprise a lot of people -- that I really heard that kind of made me listen -- I didn't hear him but once and then later on I heard him on a record -- was Earl Hines. He was playing with an orchestra out of Pittsburgh -- a singer named Louis Dippo. A lot of people never heard of him. But he was in the show Great Day in New York. He had the most powerful baritone voice I have ever heard. He used to -- Louis Dippo, Louis Dippo.

That's right. But his name, Louis; they said Louie, you know. But that's who I first heard that impressed me was Earl "Fatha" Hines. He was playing a style of piano then that was way ahead, way ahead of his time. And I didn't hear him no more until I heard him on the records with
Louie. He made records with Louie. But I heard him then and he was with this orchestra out of Pittsburgh.

Then, the next pianist that impressed me -- of course, he impressed me on the organ more than anything else. I had the first recording that Fats Waller made in 1926 on the Victor organ, the big pipe organ that Victor had. One side was Lenox Avenue Blues on one side and "St. Louis Blues" on the other. And he was the first to play jazz organ. Also, he was a good pianist, a good rhythmic pianist.
